extracted.intended_audience: agency officials, agency counsel, and administrative law practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on compliance with the Administrative Procedure Act's procedural provisions governing separation of functions, declaratory orders, appearances, investigations, subpoenas, denials, hearings, and presiding officers. Useful for agency staff drafting rules, handling adjudications, or advising on APA procedural disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of investigative/prosecuting functions (Section 5(c) disqualification)
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency officer or employee may not participate or advise in the decision, recommended decision, or agency review of an examiner's initial decision if in that or a factually related case he performed investigative or prosecuting functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if the agency's general counsel or chief accountant engaged in investigative or prosecuting functions in a case, he becomes unavailable to the agency for consultation on the decision of that or a factually related case. Such persons could still present views as witness or counsel in public proceedings, including filing briefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize staff to avoid disqualification and publish functional divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may organize staff assignments so that staff members whom it most frequently desires to consult will be free of investigative and prosecuting functions, thereby keeping them available to advise on adjudicatory decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: (1) key advisors (e.g., general counsel) remain available for difficult/novel cases rather than being disqualified by supervisory investigatory roles; (2) publishing rules identifying staff eligible to advise in decisions informs the public and assists in proving compliance with section 5(c) in litigation. Agencies should consider feasible staff organization and promulgate procedural rules reflecting separation of functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption for agency members (agency as a body) from section 5(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause 'nor shall it be applicable in any manner to the agency or any member or members of the body comprising the agency' means members of the agency itself are not precluded by section 5(c) from participating in investigation or prosecution and then in the decision of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By nature of administrative agencies where same authority may investigate/prosecute and decide, a member who actively participates in or directs an investigation will not be precluded from participating with colleagues in the decision. Legislative history supports this exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of declaratory orders (Section 5(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are authorized to issue declaratory orders 'with like effect as in the case of other orders' to terminate controversies or remove uncertainty, but only with respect to matters required by statute to be determined 'on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing' and not within the subsection's exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no statutory agency hearing procedure exists for the subject (e.g., certain SEC matters), Section 5(d) does not authorize declaratory orders. The authority is limited to matters within the Act's jurisdictional/historical scope and does not expand agency power where statute provides no hearing mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for issuing declaratory orders (sound discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may issue declaratory orders only in their 'sound discretion'; they are not required to grant every request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sound discretion means issuing declaratory orders only where both the public interest and the party's interest are protected. Necessary condition: facts must be capable of explicit statement without likelihood that subsequent events will alter them, to avoid later litigation about applicability. Agencies need not issue orders when questions will be resolved in pending administrative/judicial proceedings or when other statutory proceedings are more appropriate. Administrative issuance should follow principles governing judicial declaratory judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 6 does not override other Act provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The introductory words 'Except as otherwise provided in this Act' mean section 6's procedural rights are not intended to override contrary provisions elsewhere in the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the opportunity for informal appearance in section 6(a) should not be construed to authorize ex parte conferences during formal proceedings when such conferences are forbidden by other sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions affecting procedural rights (party/person/agency proceeding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of section 6's rights depends on definitions in section 2: 'person' includes individuals, partnerships, corporations, associations (other than agencies); 'party' includes any person or agency named or admitted as a party or properly seeking and entitled as of right to be admitted (including limited purposes); 'agency proceeding' means agency processes defined in subsections for rule making, adjudication and licensing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions determine who may claim rights such as appearance, subpoena access, and other section 6 protections; in informal rulemaking 'party' may mean any person showing requisite interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to counsel for compelled appearances (Section 6(a) formal appearance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person compelled to appear in person before any agency or representative shall be accorded the right to be accompanied, represented, and advised by counsel or, if permitted by the agency, by other qualified representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restates existing law: applies only to persons whose appearance is compelled (party or witness). Persons appearing voluntarily or at an agency's request but not compelled do not have this statutory right. 'Other qualified representative' may include non-lawyers where the agency permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of parties to appear in agency proceedings (Section 6(a) party appearance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every 'party' shall have the right to appear in any agency proceeding in person or by or with counsel or other duly qualified representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'agency proceeding' includes rule making, adjudication, and licensing, this right extends to formal and certain informal proceedings; in informal rulemaking, a person with requisite interest must be allowed to appear if the agency provides oral opportunity. Agencies retain discretion over the type of proceedings (oral vs written).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency control over practice before agencies (lawyers and non-lawyers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 6(a) leaves intact agencies' control over who may practice before them; Congress did not change existing agency powers to regulate practice by lawyers or non-lawyers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may require minimal proof of bar standing for lawyers, may exclude persons of improper character after hearing, may exclude counsel for unruly conduct, and may impose reasonable time limits on former employees practicing before the agency. Determinations about non-lawyer representation remain with agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal appearance rights and limits (Section 6(a) informal appearance)
rubrics_metrics.description: So far as the orderly conduct of public business permits, any interested person may appear before an agency or responsible officers to present, adjust, or determine any issue, request, or controversy in any proceeding or in connection with any agency function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appearance should be with a 'responsible officer or employee' capable of deciding or making recommendations — not merely mechanical staff. The right is limited by 'orderly conduct' — agencies need not permit appearances that would impair efficiency (e.g., directors need not personally meet every applicant). Agencies are not required to give notice unless they choose; repeated opportunities to present same arguments are not required; opportunity may be denied where summary action's timeliness precludes discussion (e.g., emergency public-safety actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable dispatch in concluding matters (Section 6(a) timeliness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every agency shall proceed with reasonable dispatch to conclude any matter presented to it, giving due regard to the convenience and necessity of parties or their representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a restatement of sound administrative practice; agencies must balance prompt resolution with fairness to parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigatory demands must be authorized by law (Section 6(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: No process, requirement of a report, inspection, or other investigative act or demand shall be issued, made, or enforced except as authorized by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restates existing law limiting agency investigatory power to statutory authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of compelled witnesses to copies/transcripts (Section 6(b) witness rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every person compelled to submit data or evidence shall be entitled to retain or, on payment of lawfully prescribed costs, procure a copy or transcript thereof, except that in a nonpublic investigatory proceeding the witness may be limited for good cause to inspection of the official transcript of his testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Right extends only to data/evidence submitted by that witness, and only to persons compelled to submit (not volunteers). Limitation for confidentiality: where prosecutions may follow, sharing copies could harm law enforcement; in such situations inspection-only is permissible for good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability and limits of administrative subpoenas to parties (Section 6(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency subpoenas authorized by law shall be issued to any party upon request and, as may be required by rules of procedure, upon a statement or showing of general relevance and reasonable scope of the evidence sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to both subpoenas ad testificandum and duces tecum. Agencies that have subpoena power should publish rules specifying how parties request subpoenas and what the request must state. Subpoenas must meet 'general relevance and reasonable scope' interpreted in light of making subpoenas equally available to private parties; agencies may refuse to issue subpoenas so irrelevant or unreasonable that a court would refuse enforcement. Section does not create subpoena power where none exists by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial enforcement standard for subpoenas (Section 6(c) enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon contest the court shall sustain any such subpoena or similar process or demand to the extent that it is found to be in accordance with law, and in enforcement proceedings shall issue an order requiring appearance or production within a reasonable time, under penalty for contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This adopts existing law on subpoenas; it does not expand judicial inquiry beyond established limits (e.g., courts do not resolve threshold jurisdictional questions unrelated to subpoena enforcement). 'In accordance with law' refers to statutes administered by the agency and relevant judicial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt notice and statement of grounds for denial (Section 6(d) denials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt notice shall be given of the denial in whole or in part of any written application, petition, or other request of any interested person made in connection with any agency proceeding; except in affirming a prior denial or where denial is self-explanatory, such notice shall be accompanied by a simple statement of procedural or other grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to requests related to rulemaking, adjudication, and licensing (formal or informal). Notice may be written or oral; the statement of grounds must be sufficient to advise the party of the general basis for denial. Does not apply to matters unrelated to rulemaking/adjudication/licensing routine agency matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may preside at hearings (Section 7(a) presiding officers)
rubrics_metrics.description: There shall preside at the taking of evidence: (1) the agency, (2) one or more members of the body which comprises the agency, or (3) one or more examiners appointed as provided in the Act; but the Act does not supersede conduct of specified classes of proceedings by boards or officers specially provided for by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exception permits hearings before statutory boards or designated officers (including joint boards), and does not authorize dispensing with examiners appointed under section 11 where section 11 applies. Where a statute authorizes hearings by particular officers, that may have implications for applicability of separation-of-function rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality of presiding officers and participants (Section 7(a) impartiality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The functions of all presiding officers and of officers participating in decisions in conformity with section 8 shall be conducted in an impartial manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They must act impartially rather than as representatives of investigative or prosecuting authority, but may question witnesses, ensure necessary evidence is adduced, and keep hearings orderly and efficient. The impartiality requirement does not prohibit active management to develop a complete record.
